content: Exercise hypertension refers to an abnormal and excessive increase in blood pressure during physical activity. Individuals with exercise hypertension often experience spikes in systolic blood pressure that reach 250 mmHg or higher. A systolic blood pressure rise exceeding 200 mmHg during exercise at a workload of 100 watts is considered pathological. If the systolic pressure rises above 220 mmHg, it typically requires pharmacological intervention to manage the condition effectively. In healthy individuals, the diastolic blood pressure response to moderate-intensity dynamic exercises, such as walking or running, generally remains stable or may slightly decrease due to improved blood flow. However, in some cases, a diastolic pressure increase of 10 mmHg or more has been observed. Recent research conducted at Johns Hopkins University, involving a cohort of athletes aged 55 to 75 with mild hypertension, has identified a correlation between exercise hypertension and a reduced ability of major blood vessels to adapt their size in response to increased blood flow. This phenomenon is likely attributed to impaired endothelial cell function within the vessel walls. It is important to distinguish this condition from vascular stiffness, as no correlation was found between blood vessel wall stiffness and the observed effects of exercise hypertension.
